newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iran conference urges halt to Afghan war.
newsitem.headline: Iran conference urges halt to Afghan war.

text.p: A regional conference held in Tehran called on Wednesday for an immediate halt to fighting in Afghanistan and urged the warring factions to seek a negotiated solution to the crisis.
A statement issued at the end of the two-day gathering hosted by Iran said the participants supported efforts, especially by the United Naitons, to hold an international conference on Afghanistan.

Representatives from the United Nations, India, Turkey, Russia, China, Central Asian republics, the European Union and the Organisation of the Islamic Conference (OIC) attended the conference which opened on Tuesday.
Pakistan, a key player in neighbouring Afghanistan, stayed away from the conference. Saudi Arabia and Uzbekistan were invited but did not attend.

"The conference calls for an immediate end to military confrontation and requests that warring Afghan sides avoid using violence and adopt negotiations and peaceful means to reach a lasting political solution and the creation of an all-party government," the statement said.
It said the conference recommended further discussions "in the region and within the framework of the United Nations to review ways to end the conflict".
Iran's Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati told a news conference later that the aim of the meeting was to draw the world's attention to the conflict.
The ousted government of Afghan President Burhanuddin Rabbani, which Iran backs, did not take part in the conference, nor did the Taleban which Tehran brands as "rebels" and other Afghan groups.
Velayati said that Pakistan's absence was not an indication that "our relations are unfriendly".
Iranian media have accused Pakistan of setting up the Sunni Moslem Taleban with backing from the United States and funding from Saudi Arabia to counter Iran's influence in the region.
Pakistan, which plays an active role in Afghanistan, denies the charge and says it has no favourites among Afghan factions.
Pakistan said on Sunday it would not attend, citing problems with the agenda and guest list, which included arch-foe India.

Pakistan and Iran worked closely together in diplomatic moves over Afghanistan during 17 years of civil war there, but differences appeared between them after the recent emergence of the Taleban as a new force in Afghan politics.
